persona.name: Anjali Gupta
persona.background: She drives long hours in heavy traffic and often skips meals and rest breaks, making fatigue and heat exposure common during her workday.

diagnoses.name: Multiple sclerosis (Relapsing-remitting MS)
diagnoses.description: A demyelinating disease with relapsing and remitting symptoms disseminated in time and space; common presentations include optic neuritis, sensory symptoms (e.g., Lhermitte’s sign), brainstem syndromes (diplopia/vertigo with nystagmus), ataxia, urinary symptoms, fatigue, and Uhthoff’s phenomenon; MRI shows multifocal T2 lesions (often periventricular Dawson’s fingers) and CSF may show oligoclonal IgG bands and raised IgG index.

diagnoses.name: Acute brainstem stroke (Posterior circulation stroke—POCS)
diagnoses.description: Posterior circulation strokes can present with brainstem or cerebellar signs such as dizziness/imbalance and nystagmus; CT is used initially to identify/exclude hemorrhage.

diagnoses.name: Wallenberg’s syndrome (Lateral medullary syndrome)
diagnoses.description: A vertebral artery/PICA territory brainstem syndrome with nystagmus, cerebellar ataxia, lateropulsion and other lateral medullary signs; a posterior circulation stroke syndrome.

diagnoses.name: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)
diagnoses.description: Due to a medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) lesion, causing ipsilateral adduction palsy with contralateral gaze-evoked nystagmus; can occur with demyelinating disease.

diagnoses.name: Multiple sclerosis (Relapsing-remitting MS)
diagnoses.description: Relapsing and remitting CNS white matter symptoms with dissemination in time and space; typical MRI T2 hyperintense multifocal lesions (periventricular/juxtacortical/infratentorial/spinal cord) and supportive CSF findings (raised IgG index/oligoclonal bands).

diagnoses.name: Acute transverse myelitis
diagnoses.description: A noncompressive myelopathy that may have acute onset and early bladder/bowel involvement.

diagnoses.name: Subacute combined degeneration of cord (Vitamin B12 deficiency)
diagnoses.description: A treatable myelopathy with paresthesia in hands/feet, early loss of vibration and position sensation, progressive spastic and ataxic weakness; a key clue is loss of reflexes from superimposed peripheral neuropathy with Babinski’s sign; MRI may show T2 hyperintensity along posterolateral columns (inverted V/rabbit ear sign).

diagnoses.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS)
diagnoses.description: A progressive disorder with simultaneous UMN and LMN involvement, spreading weakness with wasting and fasciculations; sensory is typically not involved and bladder/bowel are rarely involved.

diagnoses.name: Migraine with aura (Classical migraine)
diagnoses.description: Episodic severe headache often unilateral with warning aura (commonly visual) before headache; associated with sensitivity to light/sound/movement and nausea/vomiting.

diagnoses.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus
diagnoses.description: Enlarged ventricles with normal opening pressure presenting with the triad of dementia, gait disturbance, and urinary incontinence (Adams triad).

precomputedExplanations.description: **Relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS)** is an immune-mediated **demyelinating** disease of the CNS causing neurologic deficits separated in time and CNS location. It typically presents with discrete relapses (e.g., **optic neuritis**, sensory symptoms, ataxia) followed by partial or complete recovery, with characteristic MRI and CSF inflammatory markers.
keySymptoms: **Lhermitte’s sign** - Electric shock sensation down spine/limbs with neck flexion from cervical demyelination.
**Optic neuritis** - Subacute painful monocular vision loss, reduced color vision, and afferent pupillary defect.
**Uhthoff’s phenomenon** - Transient worsening of neurologic symptoms with heat/exertion due to impaired conduction.
**Ataxia/unsteadiness** - Gait imbalance from cerebellar or sensory pathway involvement during demyelinating relapse.
**Fatigue** - Disproportionate, persistent tiredness common in MS, often worsened by heat and exertion.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This presentation is strongly suggestive of **CNS demyelination**: episodic neurologic symptoms with **optic neuropathy**, **ataxia**, and **Lhermitte’s sign** imply lesions in different CNS locations. Heat-related visual worsening supports **Uhthoff’s phenomenon**, classically seen in **MS**. Typical supportive testing would include MRI showing multifocal **T2 hyperintense** lesions (e.g., periventricular **Dawson’s fingers**) and CSF with **oligoclonal IgG bands** and elevated **IgG index**. Overall, the symptom pattern aligns with dissemination in **space** and **time**, characteristic of RRMS.

precomputedExplanations.description: An **acute posterior circulation stroke** is a sudden ischemic event affecting the **brainstem/cerebellum** supplied by vertebrobasilar arteries. It typically causes abrupt focal neurologic deficits (e.g., vertigo, diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia) with maximal severity at onset rather than relapsing episodes.
keySymptoms: **Sudden onset focal deficits** - Symptoms reach maximum immediately, unlike gradual or fluctuating relapses.
**Vertigo/dizziness** - Acute vestibular syndrome from brainstem/cerebellar ischemia causing severe spinning sensation.
**Ataxia** - Abrupt gait and limb incoordination from cerebellar or brainstem pathway involvement.
**Diplopia/ophthalmoplegia** - Brainstem cranial nerve ischemia causing double vision and abnormal eye movements.
**Dysarthria/dysphagia** - Bulbar dysfunction from medullary/pontine involvement leading to slurred speech or choking.
**Crossed brainstem signs** - Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits with contralateral motor/sensory findings suggest brainstem lesion.

However, posterior circulation stroke classically presents with **sudden, persistent deficits** and often includes prominent brainstem cranial nerve features (e.g., **diplopia**, **dysarthria**, **dysphagia**). In this case, symptoms are **episodic/relapsing-remitting** over months and include **Lhermitte’s sign** and heat-related visual worsening (**Uhthoff’s phenomenon**), which are far more characteristic of **demyelination**. The provided MRI pattern (multifocal **T2** lesions with **Dawson’s fingers**) and CSF findings (possible **oligoclonal bands**) support **Multiple sclerosis (RRMS)** rather than acute infarction.

**Lesion pattern on MRI** - Stroke shows diffusion-restricted vascular-territory infarct; **RRMS** shows multifocal **T2** plaques (periventricular/juxtacortical/infratentorial), often **Dawson’s fingers**.
**Provoked symptoms** - Stroke is not triggered by heat/neck flexion; **RRMS** can show **Uhthoff’s phenomenon** and **Lhermitte’s sign**.
**CSF profile** - Stroke usually has normal CSF; **RRMS** may show **oligoclonal IgG bands** and elevated **IgG index**.
**Age/risk factors** - Stroke more typical with vascular risk factors; **RRMS** commonly presents in young adults, especially women.

**Vascular risk factors** - No hypertension, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation, or hypercoagulable trigger provided.
**Cranial nerve brainstem signs** - Absence of clear cranial nerve palsies reduces likelihood of brainstem stroke.

precomputedExplanations.description: Wallenberg’s syndrome is an acute ischemic stroke of the lateral medulla, most often due to vertebral artery or PICA occlusion. It causes a sudden-onset “crossed” brainstem syndrome with ipsilateral cranial nerve findings and contralateral sensory deficits, rather than relapsing demyelinating episodes.
keySymptoms: **Acute vertigo/dizziness** - Sudden severe spinning sensation from vestibular nucleus involvement, typically abrupt onset.
**Nystagmus** - Involuntary rhythmic eye movements due to vestibular pathway disruption in the lateral medulla.
**Ipsilateral facial pain/temperature loss** - Spinal trigeminal nucleus lesion causes reduced facial pinprick and temperature sensation.
**Contralateral body pain/temperature loss** - Spinothalamic tract involvement reduces pain and temperature on opposite body side.
**Dysphagia/hoarseness** - Nucleus ambiguus involvement produces swallowing difficulty and voice changes, often prominent early.
**Ipsilateral Horner syndrome** - Sympathetic pathway disruption causes ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis on the same side.
**Ipsilateral limb ataxia** - Inferior cerebellar peduncle involvement causes incoordination on the lesion side.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This diagnosis is considered when a patient has a sudden-onset brainstem syndrome with vertigo, nystagmus, dysphagia/hoarseness, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, and possible ipsilateral Horner syndrome. The pattern reflects a focal vascular lesion in the lateral medulla with “crossed” findings. Neuroimaging typically shows an acute infarct in the lateral medulla on diffusion-weighted MRI. The course is usually monophasic and acute rather than episodic relapses separated by recovery.

**Pathophysiology** - Wallenberg’s is focal ischemia (PICA/vertebral artery); **RRMS** is CNS demyelination with dissemination in time/space.
**Signature symptoms** - Wallenberg’s features dysphagia/hoarseness and crossed sensory loss; **RRMS** features optic neuritis, Lhermitte’s, Uhthoff’s.
**Imaging pattern** - Wallenberg’s shows lateral medullary infarct on DWI; **RRMS** shows multifocal **T2** lesions (e.g., periventricular **Dawson’s fingers**).
**CSF findings** - Wallenberg’s typically lacks **oligoclonal IgG bands**; **RRMS** often has oligoclonal bands and elevated **IgG index**.
missingFindings: **Dysphagia/hoarseness** - Absence of nucleus ambiguus signs argues strongly against lateral medullary infarct.
**Crossed sensory loss** - No ipsilateral facial and contralateral body pain/temperature deficit pattern described.
**Ipsilateral Horner syndrome** - No ptosis/miosis/anhidrosis reported, commonly present in Wallenberg’s.
**Acute focal brainstem stroke imaging** - Case MRI description matches demyelinating plaques, not a lateral medullary DWI infarct.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)** is an ocular motility disorder caused by a lesion of the **medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF)** in the brainstem. It produces impaired horizontal gaze coordination, classically with **adduction weakness** of the affected eye and **abducting nystagmus** of the contralateral eye.

**Abducting nystagmus** - Contralateral abducting eye shows nystagmus during attempted lateral gaze.
**Horizontal diplopia** - Double vision worse on lateral gaze due to disconjugate eye movements.
**Gaze-evoked symptoms** - Symptoms are provoked by horizontal gaze testing rather than neck flexion.
**Brainstem localization** - Findings localize to pontine/midbrain MLF, not optic nerve or spinal cord.

Clinically it presents with a characteristic eye movement pattern: impaired adduction on attempted lateral gaze with **abducting nystagmus** in the other eye. In young adults, INO is commonly caused by **multiple sclerosis**, but INO itself is a specific sign rather than a full explanation for disseminated neurologic episodes. The patient’s broader relapsing symptoms (sensory spinal cord phenomena, ataxia, optic neuritis/Uhthoff) point to a demyelinating disease course rather than an isolated ocular motility syndrome.

**Neck flexion shock** - **Lhermitte’s sign** suggests cervical cord demyelination in **RRMS**, not typical for isolated INO.

**Cognitive impairment** - Subcortical slowing, impaired attention/executive function progressing to dementia-like features over months.
**Urinary urgency/incontinence** - Early urgency and frequency progressing to incontinence due to frontal-subcortical dysfunction.
**Ventriculomegaly** - Enlarged ventricles on imaging out of proportion to cortical atrophy, supporting hydrocephalus.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: NPH is considered when a patient develops a progressive gait disorder accompanied by cognitive decline and urinary symptoms, with neuroimaging showing ventriculomegaly. The syndrome is typically insidious rather than episodic, and it is most common in older adults. Diagnosis is supported by MRI/CT features (ventricular enlargement, tight high-convexity sulci) and improvement after large-volume lumbar tap or external lumbar drainage. Treatment is often ventriculoperitoneal shunting in appropriately selected patients.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: This 29-year-old has **relapsing/remitting focal neurologic episodes** (optic neuritis-like visual blurring with **Uhthoff’s phenomenon**, **Lhermitte’s sign**, and ataxia), which strongly suggests **multiple sclerosis** rather than a chronic gait-cognition-urinary syndrome. Her MRI description (multifocal **T2** lesions with **Dawson’s fingers**) and potential CSF **oligoclonal bands** are typical for MS, not NPH.
keyDifferencesFromCorrect: **Age group** - NPH usually affects older adults; **RRMS** commonly presents in young adults, especially women.
**Time course** - NPH is slowly progressive; **RRMS** features discrete attacks with partial/complete recovery.
**Core symptoms** - NPH triad is gait apraxia, cognitive decline, urinary incontinence; **RRMS** often has optic neuritis, sensory symptoms, ataxia, fatigue.
**Lhermitte’s sign** - Not characteristic of NPH; common in **RRMS** due to cervical spinal cord demyelination.
**Uhthoff’s phenomenon** - Not seen in NPH; supports **RRMS** with heat-sensitive conduction in demyelinated pathways.
**MRI pattern** - NPH shows ventriculomegaly; **RRMS** shows multifocal periventricular/juxtacortical/infratentorial/spinal **T2** lesions (e.g., **Dawson’s fingers**).
**CSF findings** - NPH lacks inflammatory markers; **RRMS** may show elevated **IgG index** and **oligoclonal IgG bands**.
missingFindings: **Ventriculomegaly** - No imaging description of enlarged ventricles out of proportion to atrophy, expected in NPH.
**Urinary incontinence/urgency** - Not reported; a key component of the NPH clinical triad.
**Cognitive decline** - Not reported; NPH typically includes progressive executive dysfunction and slowed processing.
**Progressive gait apraxia** - Patient reports episodic unsteadiness/ataxia rather than a persistent magnetic gait.

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about relapsing and remitting episodes affecting different CNS sites (separate attacks with recovery), including timing and whether symptoms fully resolve between episodes.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: RRMS is characterized by discrete attacks with complete recovery; MS diagnosis is suggested by relapsing/remitting symptoms referable to different areas of CNS white matter (dissemination in time and space).
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: History of discrete neurologic attacks with recovery and involvement of different neurologic functions/localizations over time (dissemination in time and space).
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS) (85–90%): Discrete attack and complete recovery.” / “relapsing and remitting symptoms referable to different areas of CNS white matter.”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about optic neuropathy (optic neuritis) symptoms such as episodes of visual disturbance.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Optic neuropathy (neuritis) is a common presentation of MS and supports localization to CNS white matter pathways.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Episodes consistent with optic neuropathy/neuritis (visual symptoms as a common MS presentation).

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask specifically about Lhermitte’s sign (electric sensation down the back/into limbs on neck flexion).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Relapsing/remitting sensory symptoms including Lhermitte’s sign are listed as common MS presentations and suggest spinal cord involvement.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Electric shock-like sensation running down the back and into a limb on neck flexion.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Relapsing/remitting sensory symptoms [e.g. Lhermitte’s sign (barber chair phenomenon, is an electrical sensation that runs down the back and into the limb on neck flexion)]”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about acute brainstem syndrome symptoms: sudden diplopia and vertigo, and whether associated with nystagmus.
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Acute brainstem syndrome is a common MS presentation and helps establish dissemination in space (infratentorial involvement).
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Sudden diplopia and vertigo (often with nystagmus).
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Acute brainstem syndrome: Sudden diplopia, and vertigo with nystagmus”

keyHistoryQuestions.action: Ask about urinary symptoms suggestive of bladder hyperreflexia and other common symptom burdens (fatigue, cognitive impairment, neuropathic pain, spasticity, sexual dysfunction).
keyHistoryQuestions.reasoning: Urinary symptoms (bladder hyperreflexia) and fatigue/cognitive impairment and other symptom burdens are listed as common MS presentations and support CNS involvement.
keyHistoryQuestions.expectedFinding: Urinary symptoms consistent with bladder hyperreflexia and/or fatigue/cognitive impairment/neuropathic pain/spasticity/sexual dysfunction.
keyHistoryQuestions.textbookReference: “Urinary symptoms—bladder hyperreflexia” / “Fatigue, cognitive impairment” / “Neuropathic pain, fatigue, spasticity, depression, sexual dysfunction”

keyExaminations.action: Perform a focused neurologic examination to localize deficits to multiple CNS white matter pathways (pyramidal tract, optic nerve, posterior cord, cerebellum, medial longitudinal fasciculus).
keyExaminations.reasoning: MS commonly involves these tracts; demonstrating involvement of different CNS sites supports dissemination in space clinically.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Neurologic deficits referable to multiple CNS white matter regions (e.g., pyramidal/posterior column/cerebellar/brainstem-MLF/optic pathway findings).
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “MS commonly involves pyramidal tract, optic nerve, posterior cord, cerebellum, and medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).”

keyExaminations.action: Examine ocular motility and cranial nerves for sixth nerve palsy and/or wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (WEBINO).
keyExaminations.reasoning: Sixth nerve palsy and WEBINO are listed as common presentations and indicate brainstem/MLF involvement.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Sixth cranial nerve palsy and/or WEBINO pattern on eye movement testing.
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Sixth cranial nerve palsy, wall-eyed bilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (WEBINO)”

keyExaminations.action: Assess gait and coordination for unsteadiness/ataxia and look for Charcot’s triad (dysarthria, ataxia, tremor).
keyExaminations.reasoning: Unsteadiness/ataxia and Charcot’s triad are listed as common MS presentations and support cerebellar involvement.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Unsteady gait/ataxia; possibly dysarthria and tremor (Charcot’s triad).
keyExaminations.textbookReference: “Unsteadiness or ataxia. Charcot’s triad of dysarthria, ataxia, and tremor”

keyExaminations.action: Evaluate for bladder dysfunction consistent with bladder hyperreflexia in the clinical assessment of symptoms.
keyExaminations.reasoning: Urinary symptoms due to bladder hyperreflexia are common in MS and may be present on clinical assessment.
keyExaminations.expectedFinding: Clinical evidence consistent with urinary symptoms/bladder hyperreflexia.

keyInvestigations.action: Order cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination including cell count, IgG/total protein, CSF IgG index, and protein electrophoresis for oligoclonal IgG bands.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: CSF may show mononuclear pleocytosis, increased IgG and IgG index, and oligoclonal IgG bands (not specific). CSF positivity is also used as part of criteria in progressive disease and helps support inflammatory demyelination.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Mononuclear pleocytosis (5–60 mononuclear cells/mm), increased IgG/CSF protein/IgG index, and oligoclonal IgG bands (may be present).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “CSF cell count may be raised (5–60 mononuclear cells/mm)—mononuclear cell pleocytosis.” / “Increased immunoglobulin G (IgG)… CSF IgG index.” / “Oligoclonal IgG bands… but these are not specific.”

keyInvestigations.action: Order evoked potentials (visual, auditory, somatosensory ± motor) to assess CNS pathway function.
keyInvestigations.reasoning: EP abnormalities occur in 80–90% of MS patients and can demonstrate involvement of CNS pathways, though less important than MRI.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Abnormalities on one or more EP modalities.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “abnormalities on one or more EP modalities occur in 80–90% of MS patients. However, they are less important than MRI.”

keyInvestigations.action: Order MRI brain and spinal cord to look for characteristic demyelinating lesions (T2 hyperintense, multifocal distribution).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: MRI shows characteristic abnormalities in >95% of MS patients; lesions are T2 hyperintense, oval up to 2 cm, often perpendicular to ventricles (Dawson’s fingers), and multifocal (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, spinal cord). MRI is central to demonstrating dissemination in space/time per McDonald criteria.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions in typical locations; Dawson’s fingers pattern may be seen.
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “Characteristic abnormalities are found in >95% of patients.” / “Lesion appears as focal area of hyperintensity on T2-weighted.” / “Dawson’s fingers.” / “Lesions are multifocal (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord).”

keyInvestigations.action: Apply McDonald criteria using clinical attacks/lesions plus MRI evidence for dissemination in space/time (and/or await further clinical attacks as specified).
keyInvestigations.reasoning: The textbook provides McDonald criteria to combine clinical attacks/lesions with MRI evidence to establish MS diagnosis.
keyInvestigations.expectedFinding: Meets one of the McDonald criteria pathways (e.g., ≥2 attacks and ≥2 lesions; or MRI evidence of dissemination in space/time as required).
keyInvestigations.textbookReference: “McDonald criteria for MS are presented in Table 16.26.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Neuromyelitis optica (Devic’s disease, NMO)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Differentiate by distribution (restricted to optic nerves and spinal cord in NMO vs any white matter in MS), MRI patterns (brain MRI usually normal in NMO vs multiple periventricular lesions in MS; cord MRI LETM with ≥3 segments in NMO vs multiple small peripheral lesions in MS), CSF profile (pleocytosis during attack and oligoclonal bands usually absent in NMO vs oligoclonal bands usually present in MS), and antibodies (anti-AQP4/anti-NMO present in NMO vs no antibodies in MS).
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: Table 16.27: “Restricted to optic nerves and spinal cord… Brain MRI usually normal… Cord MRI Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (LETM)… Oligoclonal bands Usually absent… Anti-AQP4… present… Multiple sclerosis… Any white matter… Multiple periventricular white matter lesions… Multiple small peripheral lesions… Oligoclonal bands Usually present… No antibodies.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM)
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Consider as an infectious differential listed by the textbook when evaluating demyelinating presentations; use the overall clinical pattern (MS typically shows relapsing/remitting symptoms with dissemination in time and space) and supportive MRI/CSF findings to favor MS when criteria are met.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Infectious [e.g., acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), HIV encephalitis, Creutzfeldt–Jakob encephalitis]” / “The neurological deficits are disseminated in time and space.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: HIV encephalitis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Listed as an infectious condition in the differential; favor MS when there is a relapsing-remitting course with dissemination in time/space and characteristic multifocal MRI lesions.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Infectious [e.g., … HIV encephalitis …]” / “relapsing and remitting symptoms referable to different areas of CNS white matter.”

differentialDiagnoses.name: Creutzfeldt–Jakob encephalitis
differentialDiagnoses.howToRuleOut: Listed as an infectious differential; favor MS when the course is relapsing-remitting with dissemination in time/space and MRI shows typical demyelinating lesion distribution.
differentialDiagnoses.textbookReference: “Infectious [e.g., … Creutzfeldt–Jakob encephalitis]” / “Lesions are multifocal (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial, or spinal cord).”

idealPathway.diagnosticApproach: Suspect RRMS in a young adult with relapsing-remitting neurologic symptoms referable to different CNS white matter sites (dissemination in time and space), using common presentations such as optic neuritis, Lhermitte’s sign, acute brainstem syndrome (diplopia/vertigo with nystagmus), ataxia, and urinary symptoms. Perform a focused neurologic exam targeting tracts commonly involved (pyramidal, optic nerve, posterior cord, cerebellum, MLF). Support the diagnosis with investigations: CSF analysis (mononuclear pleocytosis, increased IgG/IgG index, oligoclonal bands—nonspecific) and evoked potentials (often abnormal but less important than MRI). Confirm using MRI brain/spinal cord showing characteristic multifocal T2 hyperintense lesions (periventricular/juxtacortical/infratentorial/spinal cord) with typical features such as Dawson’s fingers, and apply McDonald criteria to establish dissemination in space/time. Differentiate from NMO using Table 16.27 MRI/CSF/antibody patterns, as IFN is contraindicated in NMO.
